summary: The note argues that nutritional therapy, the tailored use of foods and nutrients to promote health and prevent disease, is gaining support as a preventive health strategy. It cites expert statements, a research paper, and cost, accessibility and education considerations, with type 2 diabetes as an example. It concludes that research, public education and policy change are needed to establish food as medicine in healthcare.
one_line: Nutritional therapy is gaining momentum as a cost-effective, evidence-backed approach to preventing chronic disease, though accessibility, provider education and policy hurdles remain.
key_facts: Dr. Sarah Levinson, a prominent figure in preventive medicine, spoke at the Annual Health and Wellness Conference in New York on December 1, 2023.
Levinson said: "Our plates hold more than just our next meal; they hold the key to our health."
Nutritional therapy is defined as the tailored use of foods and nutrients to promote health, manage, and prevent disease.

A paper published October 15, 2023 by the Journal of Nutrition and Disease Prevention found diets rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, and seeds were associated with a reduced risk of chronic diseases.
Chronic diseases are described as the leading causes of death and disability worldwide.

Registered Dietitian Michael Thompson said on September 20, 2023 that individualizing diet plans and focusing on whole, unprocessed foods has significantly improved patients' blood sugar control without solely relying on medication.
The note argues that investing in nutritional therapies can reduce reliance on expensive medications and invasive procedures, leading to potential savings.
As reported on September 30, 2023, telehealth services offering nutritional counseling have gained popularity, improving accessibility.
The Thompson Integrative Medicine Institute, established on November 5, 2023, includes comprehensive nutritional education in its curricula.
The 'Food for Health' symposium on January 22, 2024 gathered health professionals, lawmakers, and food industry leaders.
Proponents like Levinson argue nutritional counseling should be a primary service in health systems, given its potential to prevent conditions from diabetes to heart disease.
The note says continued research, public education, and policy change are vital to cementing nutritional therapy's role in healthcare.
